title: Hepatic Encephalopathy: Acute Assessment and Precipitant Management

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with cirrhosis or portosystemic shunting who present to the emergency department (ED) or a medical ward with confusion or reduced consciousness from overt hepatic encephalopathy (HE): grading, exclusion of other causes, search for and correction of precipitants, lactulose treatment and prevention of recurrence with lactulose and rifaximin. Uses the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and European Association for the Study of the Liver (AASLD/EASL) 2014 guideline and US product labels. Acute liver failure (HE type A) is covered in a separate topic.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-21.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi hepatic encephalopathy guideline was found; AASLD/EASL 2014 is used.
AASLD/EASL 2014 says to give large parenteral doses of thiamine before glucose if Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected but gives no dose, so no thiamine regimen is listed.
AASLD/EASL 2014 gives no rifaximin dose; the dose is from the US label.
Typical adult normal ranges for ammonia, sodium, glucose and creatinine are not from AASLD/EASL; local laboratory ranges apply. Ammonia reference ranges vary with venous, arterial or plasma sampling.

pathophysiology.summary: HE is brain dysfunction caused by liver insufficiency and/or portosystemic shunting, ranging from subclinical change to coma (AASLD/EASL 2014, Definition of HE). Overt HE is a decompensating event in cirrhosis, like variceal bleeding or ascites (AASLD/EASL 2014, Epidemiology). Almost every episode has a precipitant, most often infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, diuretic overdose, electrolyte disorder or constipation (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 3). About 90% of patients improve with correction of the precipitant alone (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 16 rationale). Hyponatraemia, sepsis, renal dysfunction and diabetes increase the risk of HE (AASLD/EASL 2014, Section Alternative causes of altered mental status).

symptoms: Lethargy or apathy, disorientation for time, personality change and inappropriate behaviour (West Haven grade II) (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 2).
Somnolence to semi-stupor, confusion and gross disorientation (grade III) (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 2).
Coma with no response to pain (grade IV) (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 2).
Altered sleep rhythm, shortened attention span or euphoria in grade I (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 2).
physicalSigns: Disorientation for time: at least three of day of month, day of week, month, season or year wrong (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 2).
Disorientation for place in grade III (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 2).
Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) used when consciousness is clearly reduced (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 6).
redFlags: Grade III or IV, or unable to protect the airway: manage in an intensive care unit (ICU) setting (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 14 rationale).
Focal signs, ataxia or dysarthria: consider intracranial bleeding or Wernicke encephalopathy (AASLD/EASL 2014, Section Alternative causes of altered mental status).
Sepsis or gastrointestinal bleeding as precipitant (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 3).
Normal ammonia in suspected overt HE: re-evaluate the diagnosis (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 9).
precipitants: Overuse of lactulose causing dehydration and hypernatraemia (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 19 rationale).

differentials.condition: Alcohol intoxication, withdrawal or Wernicke encephalopathy
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Alcohol history; ataxia and eye signs cannot be told apart clinically, so give thiamine (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 4 and Section Alternative causes).
Focal signs or fall; brain imaging (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 4).

differentials.condition: Central nervous system infection or non-convulsive seizures
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fever, meningism or fluctuating consciousness (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 4).

ruleIn.testName: Infection screen: full blood count, blood and urine cultures, ascitic tap if ascites
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Raised white cells, positive cultures, ascitic neutrophils
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Infection is the most frequent precipitant of episodic HE; seek and treat it (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 3 and Recommendation 18).
ruleIn.normalValue: White cells 4.0 to 11.0 × 10⁹/L; sterile cultures (typical adult values)

clinicalManagement.title: Assess airway and level of care
actions: Grade with West Haven criteria and GCS (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 6).
Grade III or IV, or at risk of aspiration: monitor closely in an ICU setting (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 14 rationale).
If Wernicke encephalopathy is possible, give parenteral thiamine before any glucose-containing fluid (AASLD/EASL 2014, Section Alternative causes of altered mental status).

clinicalManagement.title: Look for other causes
actions: Check glucose, sodium, calcium, renal function and drug history, and image the brain if a focal or traumatic cause is possible (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 15 and Table 4).

clinicalManagement.title: Find and correct the precipitant
actions: Screen for infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, diuretic overdose, electrolyte disorder and constipation, and treat what is found (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 18 and Table 3).
Stop or reduce diuretics and sedatives contributing to the episode (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 3 and Table 4).
Avoid large volumes of non-saline fluids that cause hyponatraemia; correct severe hyponatraemia slowly (AASLD/EASL 2014, Section Alternative causes of altered mental status).

clinicalManagement.title: Start lactulose
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Once the first three steps are done
actions: Give lactulose (see Medicines); use a nasogastric tube if the patient cannot swallow safely (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 17 rationale and Recommendation 19).
Titrate to two to three soft stools a day; overuse causes aspiration, dehydration, hypernatraemia and perianal skin damage and can precipitate HE (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 19 rationale).

clinicalManagement.title: If no response
actions: Re-check for missed precipitants and alternative diagnoses (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 15).
Oral branched-chain amino acids or intravenous L-ornithine L-aspartate may be added for non-responders (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendations 21 and 22).
Recurrent intractable overt HE with liver failure is an indication for liver transplant referral (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 13).

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent recurrence
actions: Continue lactulose after the first episode (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 25).
Add rifaximin after a second episode (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 26).
Energy 35 to 40 kcal/kg ideal body weight and protein 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg per day, small frequent meals and a late-night snack (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendations 30 to 32).

regimens.patientGroup: Adults with cirrhosis and overt HE
regimens.dose: 25 mL every 1 to 2 hours until at least two soft or loose stools a day, then reduce and titrate to two to three stools a day (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 19 rationale, p. 26).
regimens.duration: Until the episode resolves, then continue as prevention
adjustments: Do not escalate to very large doses when smaller doses fail; overuse can precipitate HE (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 19 rationale).
Use with caution in diabetes (Lactulose label, Section Precautions).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Stool frequency, aiming for two to three soft stools a day (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 19 rationale).
Sodium, potassium and hydration status (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 19 rationale; Lactulose label, Section Adverse Reactions).
contraindications: Patients who need a low-galactose diet (Lactulose label, Section Contraindications).
Hydrogen gas build-up: take care with electrocautery during endoscopy (Lactulose label, Section Warnings).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Signs of brain dysfunction in a patient with liver insufficiency and/or portosystemic shunting after exclusion of other causes (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendations 2 and 4).
Disorientation or asterixis (West Haven grade II or higher) (AASLD/EASL 2014, Table 2).
West Haven grades I to IV, plus GCS when consciousness is reduced (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 6 and Table 2).
Bouts within 6 months or less of each other (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 1 rationale).

teaching.scope: Adults with cirrhosis or portosystemic shunting who present to the emergency department (ED) or a medical ward with confusion or reduced consciousness from overt hepatic encephalopathy (HE): grading, exclusion of other causes, search for and correction of precipitants, lactulose treatment and prevention of recurrence with lactulose and rifaximin. Uses the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and European Association for the Study of the Liver (AASLD/EASL) 2014 guideline and US product labels. Acute liver failure (HE type A) is covered in a separate topic.
learningObjectives: Grade HE with the West Haven criteria.
Dose lactulose to two to three soft stools a day; add rifaximin after a second episode.
pitfalls: Missing infection or bleeding as the trigger.
Escalating lactulose until the patient is dehydrated and hypernatraemic.
Attributing focal signs to HE without brain imaging.
keyPoints: Most episodes resolve when the precipitant is corrected.
Ammonia does not stage HE; a normal value questions the diagnosis.
Give thiamine before glucose if Wernicke is possible.

patientEducation: Confusion from liver disease is often triggered by infection, bleeding, constipation or water tablets.
Take lactulose every day and aim for two to three soft stools.
Family should seek help early for sleepiness, confusion or personality change.
lifestyleAndDiet: Energy 35 to 40 kcal/kg ideal body weight and protein 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg a day; do not restrict protein (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendations 30 and 31).
Small meals through the day and a late-night snack (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 32).
mdtReferrals: Emergency physician; hepatologist or gastroenterologist; ICU for grade III to IV; dietitian (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendations 30 to 33); liver transplant centre for recurrent intractable HE (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendation 13).
dischargeCriteria: Oriented, no asterixis, precipitant treated, eating, two to three soft stools a day on lactulose, carers taught warning signs, hepatology follow-up booked.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Hepatology clinic for prevention plan (lactulose; add rifaximin after a second episode), nutrition review and transplant assessment if HE is recurrent with liver failure (AASLD/EASL 2014, Recommendations 13, 25 and 26).
